title: K-T-N

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-D-L: gadol, great, and the verb to grow. Your line was grow. What did you help grow? Today, the root on the other side of the scale. Day one thousand four hundred two.

A prophet stands in a farmhouse in Bethlehem with a horn of oil, looking for a king. The farmer, Jesse, brings out his sons, one after another, tall ones, impressive ones. Each time the answer is no. Finally the prophet asks whether these are all the children. And Jesse says, in effect, well, there's still the youngest, out with the sheep. In Hebrew he calls him ha-katan. The small one. Nobody thought to invite him. That small one is David. Today's root is the one Jesse used for the boy he left in the field.
screen: `A HORN OF OIL IN BETHLEHEM.` → `SEVEN SONS, ALL NO.` → `THERE'S STILL THE SMALL ONE.`

segments.voice: K-T-N. Kuf, tet, nun. Katan: small, little, young. Turn it a few ways. First, the sky. Yesterday's root sits in Genesis next to today's: God made the two great lights, "the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night." The greater is gadol. The lesser is katan. A midrash in the Talmud tells that the moon objected to sharing the sky as an equal, and was told to make itself smaller. And then, the story goes, the moon was comforted: the righteous, it was told, would be called by its name, David the small. So the small light and the small boy end up in the same story. Second, Jacob. On his way home, afraid of his brother, he prays, and the Hebrew has him say katonti, I am small, before all the kindness and truth God has shown him. A man with flocks and two camps of people, saying: I'm too small for all this. Third, the prophet Zechariah, watching a modest rebuilding that looked like nothing: "For who hath despised the day of small things?" The word for small things is from this root. Fourth, the street. In Jewish law, a katan is a minor, a child not yet obligated in the commandments. In the sayings of the fathers, the teaching is to be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one, because you don't know the reward of each. Small doesn't mean it doesn't count. Small is often where it starts.
screen: `THE LESSER LIGHT: KATAN.` · `JACOB: I AM TOO SMALL.` · `THE DAY OF SMALL THINGS.` · `A LIGHT COMMANDMENT, HANDLED WITH CARE.` · then, large: `SMALL STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Look around you for something small that does a job nobody thanks it for. A button. A hinge. A cup. A light switch. Rest your eyes on it. Notice its size, its color, how long it's been doing its work. If it's close, touch it. Then widen it to a person: someone easy to overlook in your day, whose name you may barely know, who keeps things running. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can say a word of thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
screen: `FIND ONE SMALL THING.` · `NOTICE IT.` · `ONE SMALL PERSON, TOO.`

segments.voice: K-T-N. Kuf, tet, nun: the root of katan, small, the lesser light, the youngest son, the day of small things. Today's word.
Your line: small. Today, do one small thing all the way: a dish properly washed, a short message answered properly. Day one thousand four hundred two.

notes: Editor pass: practice no longer calls a person 'small'; reworded to 'someone easy to overlook'. Other claims checked against cited texts; no other changes.

1 Samuel 16:10–11 paraphrased: Jesse makes seven sons pass before Samuel; Samuel asks if these are all; Jesse: 'there remaineth yet the youngest (ha-katan), and, behold, he keepeth the sheep'. The hook screen says 'seven sons' from 16:10. Confirm.
Genesis 1:16 fragment quoted as JPS 1917 (KJV identical for this phrase). Confirm.

Chullin 60b midrash on the moon paraphrased: the moon asks whether two kings can share one crown, is told to diminish itself, and is consoled that the righteous are called by its name (Jacob the small, Samuel the small, David the small). Confirm the paraphrase.
Genesis 32:11 (JPS numbering; KJV 32:10): katonti, 'I am not worthy' in the old translations, literally 'I am small'. Paraphrased. The 'two camps' detail is from the same verse.
Zechariah 4:10 quoted from KJV; 'small things' is ketanot. Confirm.
Katan as a halakhic minor: standard usage; confirm phrasing.
Pirkei Avot 2:1 paraphrased (be as careful with a light mitzvah as with a weighty one, for you do not know the reward of mitzvot). Confirm.
